judgments.reasoning_cat1: The grant covers 'Forgery or alteration of a Financial Instrument' and then says 'including' three check-specific illustrations, a classic general-plus-enumerated-list problem about whether the coverage reaches beyond negotiable instruments; 'direct loss' compounds it.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Its reach depends entirely on the defined terms Forgery and Financial Instrument in Subsection 11 and is cut back by Exclusion 16, and it must be squared with Insuring Clauses 5 and 6, which cover electronic frauds — a boundary a court would have to draw.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A single sentence resting on 'direct loss' and 'Computer Fraud committed by a Third Party'; whether a fraudulently induced but voluntary transfer is a 'direct loss' from computer fraud is precisely the kind of phrase two parties read differently.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Its scope is set by the Computer Fraud, Computer Violation and Computer System definitions and is bounded by Exclusions 12(k), 15 and 17 and the privacy endorsement, whose carve-back preserves only Insuring Clause 6 — leaving the Clause 5/Clause 6 boundary contestable.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Turns on 'direct loss of Money' 'resulting from Funds Transfer Fraud', and the defined term requires instructions issued 'without such Organization's knowledge or consent' — a phrase that squarely divides authorised-but-deceived transfers from unauthorised ones.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It overlaps Insuring Clause 5 and is expressly the sole survivor of the privacy/data-breach endorsement carve-back, so its relationship to Clause 5 and to Exclusion 15 must be worked out.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A one-line grant keyed to a tightly drafted defined term about post office money orders and counterfeit currency; little room for competing readings.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Exclusion 12(k) expressly carves this clause back into coverage, showing deliberate coordination rather than conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A short grant resting on the defined Credit Card Fraud; the definition itself is limited to forgery of a written instrument.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Exclusion 18 excludes loss from 'any forgery or alteration of, on or in any written instrument' unless two conditions are met, which comes close to swallowing the grant — a genuine tension worth noting.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'not in collusion with such Client's employees' is a precise limiter and Theft, Forgery, Employee and Client are all defined.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It coordinates with the Ownership provision's second paragraph and with Exclusions 12(c), 12(n) and 13, all of which name Insuring Clause 9 expressly.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The final sentence says no Retention applies, while (a) and (b) require the underlying loss to exceed the Retention — readable but internally awkward, and the retention/limit references need the Declarations.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The Declarations for the Crime section list values for Items 2(A)-(J) and Item 3 in a garbled column, so which figure is the Insuring Clause 10 limit and which the Retention is not entirely transparent.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'or similar financial institution' is a catch-all after two specifics, but the class is obvious and rarely contested.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Used only in Insuring Clause 2 and consistently with the Premises definition.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'under written contract or for a fee' is a definite two-branch test.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Coheres with Insuring Clause 9, the Ownership provision and the exclusion of Client expenses from Investigative and Computer Violation Expenses.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'unlawful taking or the fraudulently induced transfer ... resulting from a Computer Violation' is the crux term; 'fraudulently induced transfer' and the causal 'resulting from' are exactly what parties dispute in spoofed-email losses.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is meaningless without the Computer Violation and Computer System definitions, and its interaction with Funds Transfer Fraud (which excludes Forgery) and with Exclusion 17 makes its perimeter a whole-instrument question.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The proviso 'owned and operated or leased and operated by an Organization' is a real lexical crux — whether a hosted or third-party-administered email system qualifies is genuinely arguable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It controls the reach of Computer Violation and hence Insuring Clause 5 and the Data and Computer Violation Expenses definitions, so the whole computer-crime scheme turns on it.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'fraudulent entry of Data into ... a Computer System' and 'change to Data elements or program logic', capped by 'directed against an Organization', are open-textured; whether spoofed message content is a fraudulent entry of Data is squarely contestable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Its meaning depends on Computer System and Data, and the trailing 'directed against an Organization' arguably modifies only (c), a general-versus-specific problem that only appears when read with Insuring Clause 5.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'reasonable expenses' and 'substantially the same level or operational capability' are soft standards, though the clause is otherwise carefully bounded by the consent requirement.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It ties into Insuring Clause 10(b), Exclusion 12(g)'s carve-back and Exclusion 12(h)'s data-cost exclusions, which fit together without contradiction.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Defines the fraud by reference to the defined Forgery of a written instrument, a narrow and definite formulation.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It works with Insuring Clause 8, Exclusion 18 and the Legal Expenses Extension 22(b), which all speak of the same written instrument.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'representation of information, knowledge, facts, concepts or instructions' is broad but is a list of near-synonyms rather than a genuine ambiguity; 'ina Computer System' is an OCR slip only.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Because Data must be 'processed and stored in a Computer System', it inherits the ownership proviso of that definition and so shapes Computer Violation and Insuring Clause 5.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'facts which would cause a reasonable person to assume' is an objective but fact-sensitive trigger, and the clause carefully includes three categories and one exclusion.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Discovery is the pivot of Exclusion 19, Subsection 25 as amended by Endorsement 3, Subsection 27's ninety-day and two-year clocks and Subsection 28's valuation dates, and those provisions do not all use it consistently.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Four enumerated categories with concrete tests (Salary, right to govern and direct); the enumeration is closed rather than catch-all.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Exclusion 13(a) excludes loss caused by agents, independent contractors and 'other similar representatives', which sits at the boundary of the leased/temporary employees included here.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Defined wholly by reference to ERISA Title 1 bonding requirements; externally fixed.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Coheres with Subsection 21 and the Insured definition, both of which treat ERISA Plans as insureds only for Insuring Clause 1.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: An enumerated list of offices with an 'equivalent positions' extension for foreign entities, which is a modest general-after-specific formulation.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Endorsement No. 1 to the Crime section rewrites subparagraph (a) to add 'trustee', so the unendorsed text as printed no longer states the operative definition.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'check, draft or similar written promise, order or direction to pay a sum certain in Money' is an enumerated list closed by 'similar', and whether an email payment instruction falls inside is exactly the contested question.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It defines the object of Insuring Clause 4 and the Legal Expenses Extension 22(a), and its narrow written-instrument focus must be reconciled with the electronic-fraud clauses 5 and 6.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'signing of the name of another natural person or organization' plus the carve-out for signatures including one's own name is a live lexical crux — whether spoofed sender names or unsigned electronic messages count is genuinely arguable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Forgery is expressly excepted from Funds Transfer Fraud and drives Insuring Clauses 1, 4 and 9 and Exclusions 12(c), 13 and 14, so its reach reallocates coverage across the section.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'purportedly issued by an Organization' and 'without such Organization's knowledge or consent' can be read consistently or in tension, and the parenthetical '(other than Forgery)' adds a further boundary; this is a genuinely contestable definition.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is the sole coverage preserved by the privacy/data-breach endorsement's carve-back and overlaps Computer Fraud, so the Clause 5/Clause 6 and Forgery boundaries must be drawn across provisions.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'designated to represent an Insured for the purpose of effecting and maintaining insurance' is definite, if it assumes a designation was made.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It matters for the Discovery definition and Exclusion 13(b), which impute awareness to the Insured, and works consistently there.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A short definition limiting plan insureds to Insuring Clause 1; unambiguous on its face.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Insuring Clause 1 pays the Parent Organization for loss sustained by 'an Insured', which Subsection 21 then rewrites for ERISA Plans; the Non-ERISA Plan branch has no corresponding amendment, a small asymmetry.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Defines start and end of conveyance precisely and identifies the custodians; little interpretive room.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Fits Insuring Clause 3 and Exclusion 14(b)'s carrier carve-out; the phrase 'outside the Premises' also coordinates with the Premises definition.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'reasonable expenses' with a consent precondition; a familiar and workable standard.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Coordinates with Insuring Clause 10(a) and Exclusion 12(g)'s carve-back consistently.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Four concrete nouns with no catch-all; about as definite as a definition gets.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Used throughout without variance, and Property is defined as tangible property 'other than Money or Securities', keeping the categories exclusive.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Two specific fact patterns, each closely described; 'good faith acceptance' is the only soft element.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Insuring Clause 7 and the carve-back in Exclusion 12(k) both track it exactly.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Mirror image of the ERISA Plan definition and equally externally anchored.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Non-ERISA Plans are Insureds for Insuring Clause 1 but Subsection 21's amendments and retention waiver apply only to ERISA Plans, leaving them without the parallel treatment.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A pure pointer to Item 4 of the Declarations; nothing to construe in the wording.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Item 4 reads 'Medidate Solutions, Inc., and its subsidiaries' — a misspelling of the named Parent Organization and an open-ended 'subsidiaries' reference that sits against the Subsidiary definition and the Changes in Exposure provision.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'interior portion of a building occupied by an Organization in conducting its business' is concrete.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with Insuring Clauses 2 and 3, Safe Burglary and the Ownership proviso on damage to Premises.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A short exclusionary definition; 'tangible property' is a settled concept.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Keeps Money, Securities and Property mutually exclusive across the insuring clauses, though it means intangible assets fall outside Insuring Clause 5 entirely.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'by violence or threat of violence, committed in the presence and cognizance of' is specific; the parenthetical excepting watchmen, porters and janitors is a closed list.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Coordinates with Insuring Clauses 2 and 3, Exclusion 12(n)'s Robbery carve-out and Exclusion 15's 'as distinct from Robbery'.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'forcible or violent entry evidenced by visible marks' is a demanding but definite evidentiary test.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Ties cleanly to Insuring Clause 2(ii) and (iv) and to the fire exclusion's carve-back for fire applied for Safe Burglary purposes.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: An inclusive list ('including bonus, commission, incentive payments, and the cost of health, welfare and pension benefits') that is open-ended, but only for a peripheral term.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Used in the Employee definition and in Exclusion 12(a)'s proviso; consistent in both.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Contains the misprint 'nor-negotiable' for 'non-negotiable' — a mechanical error, though the intended meaning is obvious in context.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with the valuation rules in Subsection 28(a) and with the Money/Property split.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A precise majority-ownership test with 'directly or indirectly, in any combination' as its only elastic element.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Item 4 of the Crime Declarations designates the parent 'and its subsidiaries' as Organizations, which together with Subsection 23 leaves a circularity about when a subsidiary becomes an Organization.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'unlawful taking' is the core term, deliberately narrower than fraud generally; the clause is otherwise tightly scoped to two insuring clauses.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Subsection 21(a) replaces Theft with 'a fraudulent or dishonest act' for ERISA Plan losses, showing the drafters knew Theft is narrower, so the provisions cohere.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A two-branch negative definition limited to natural persons; definite, though the natural-person limit excludes entity wrongdoers.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Every Insuring Clause from 2 through 8 requires a Third Party, so the natural-person restriction quietly narrows all of them, but that is consistent drafting rather than conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'resulting directly or indirectly from any authorized or unauthorized trading' is very broad, and 'trading' is undefined; the proviso then adds a detailed improper-gain measure.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The 'directly or indirectly' causation here is broader than the 'direct loss' trigger in the insuring clauses, a familiar tension but not a contradiction.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'other confidential information of any kind' is an unbounded catch-all after two specifics — a textbook general-versus-specific problem.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Endorsement/Rider No. 2 to the Crime section expressly deletes Exclusion 12(b) and substitutes new privacy exclusions, so this printed text is no longer operative — a direct clash on the face of the instrument.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A precise proportional formula keyed to ownership percentage and audited financials; mechanical rather than ambiguous.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It presupposes partners, and the Executive definition includes partners while Employee includes Executives acting in employee roles, so the interaction with Insuring Clause 1 needs care but is workable.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A long enumerated list of war-like perils closed by 'any act or condition incident to any of the foregoing', which is an open-ended catch-all whose reach is uncertain.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The terrorism disclosure notice states that terrorism coverage is made available, which pulls against a broad reading of this exclusion.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Standard nuclear exclusion with the same 'incident to any of the foregoing' tail, but the enumerated perils are technically well understood.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Nothing elsewhere in the policy grants nuclear-related coverage, so there is no counterpull.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'loss of income not realized as the result of a covered loss' is compressed and awkwardly phrased, but its intent to bar lost profits is discernible.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Reinforces the 'direct loss' trigger in the insuring clauses and overlaps Exclusion 12(g); the overlap is cumulative rather than conflicting.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'indirect or consequential loss or damage of any kind' is broad and undefined, and the boundary between indirect loss and covered 'direct loss' is a perennially litigated line.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Its carve-back preserves Insuring Clause 10 expenses only, so it must be read against the 'direct loss' language of Insuring Clauses 1 through 9 — the very causation question at the heart of the computer-fraud clauses.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Four specific data-cost scenarios, each concretely described; 'knowingly used illegal copies' is the only fact-laden term.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It trims the Computer Violation Expenses definition and Insuring Clause 10(b), consistently with their consent and reproduction limits.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A clear exclusion of litigation costs with a single named carve-back; nothing vague.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The carve-back points to Subsection 22, which exists and matches, so the cross-reference holds.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The extracted text mislabels the paragraph '(i)' where the body twice refers to 'Exclusion 12(j)' — a mechanical inconsistency, though the carve-backs themselves are specific.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The lettering slip also matters because Exclusion 12(i) genuinely exists and covers legal fees, so a reader tracing references could be misled.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'knowingly having given or surrendered' in 'any exchange or purchase' is broad and the knowledge element is fact-sensitive; the carve-backs are precise, however.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It preserves Insuring Clause 7 and Property losses under Insuring Clause 5 but not Money losses under Clause 5, which bears directly on fraudulently induced transfers under the Computer Fraud definition.
